title: Non-Bib Shorts With Pockets: Round-Up Review – Travis Engel
content:
If you’ve ever felt marginalized for not liking bib shorts, you came to the right place. Although Travis will happily strap up for local rides, he prefers the freedom and convenience of non-bib shorts on multi-day adventures. They just need to have pockets, like the four we review here.

Bibs are great. They take the pressure off your midsection and allow for some vertical cross-ventilation. They can offer tight-fitting lumbar pockets and a more stationary chamois. But as a mountain biker living in these packless times, bibs sacrifice the feeling of comfort and freedom I’m so used to. I hadn’t thought of this until I noticed that my pinkies and ring fingers get a little numb on long rides. That was less severe and more delayed when I wasn’t wearing bibs. My physiology may play a role there, including my mismatched combo of an XL-height torso and LG-diameter waist. Sizing down tends to be great on my hips but tight on my shoulders.

But even my broken-in, sheer-strapped, $250 Gore Bike Wear bibs (RIP) aren’t as liberating as the old-school bottoms I reserve for bikepacking. And of course, bibs are cumbersome when donning and doffing. Even with my convenient male anatomy, that’s an extra faff on tours when my riding clothes are my only clothes until I get to camp. So, I wanted to shed some light on this forgotten class of shorts.

At first, this was going to be a listicle. I thought the category would be too crowded for a proper group review. How could I say something unique about each one of the dozens of non-bib shorts out there? The list of apparel brands I started with was stacked 32 lines high. That list got a little shorter when I learned some brands don’t even make non-bib shorts. It got shorter still when I cut the brands who only make “liner” shorts. But the final elimination round came when I remembered how much I love tights with hip pockets.

On mid-sized rides, it doesn’t bother me to have my phone in there for responding to texts or selecting podcasts. Honestly, when I inevitably forget it’s in there, it doesn’t bother me on long rides either. And pockets are really useful when staging and de-staging. If there’s a drive or a grocery run before and/or after a ride, it’s nice to have somewhere other than my hip pack or frame bag to put my wallet and keys. So, hip pockets were a must. And that left me with five options … which dropped to four when one brand went radio-silent. So, here we are.

Rapha Core Cargo

  • 13mm chamois thickness
  • 181g (size large)
  • Overlock seams
  • 24cm inseam
  • 26cm center to top front
  • 28cm center to top rear
  • Fit is true to size
  • Black, Dark Navy (tested)
  • $160

I weighed all the shorts to help quantify how minimalist or maximalist each one might feel. And I wasn’t surprised that the Rapha Core Cargo were the lightest. They have the most barely-there feel, like they’re painted on. They seem the most flexible, too. I didn’t have to go around carefully plucking every panel after climbing in for them to feel “centered.”

The chamois was also on the thin side. And you can tell when you ride in it. The pad’s flat structure and simple, foam-like material aren’t doing anything magical to feel more plush than their thickness would indicate. So, it won’t convert anyone who needs that pillow-top experience. But it immediately feels less diaper-like. They’re more natural when sitting down during a break or hiking up a steep section.

Structurally, the Core Cargos are pretty unique. They have the highest waist in the bunch, but I found you can scrunch it down an inch with no issues. There’s a noticeable peak in tension at the uppermost rim of the waist, but it wasn’t as severe as it was on the MBO Prime Cargo. And I fixed it by overstretching it until I heard a couple snaps. I’m probably not supposed to, but I’ve done it for years on waistbands and bib straps without quickening their demise.

There’s also the silicone traction treatment on the back of the waist. No other non-bib shorts I tested had that. Maybe it’s not ideal if you’ve got a hairy back, but I couldn’t tell ya. Another novel feature was the mesh pockets. That improved ventilation when I left them empty. It also made for a neat perspective-fade effect on the neat Rapha logos.

Pros:

  • Sleek, barely-there feel
  • Good overall ventilation
  • Minimal chamois is all that (most) riders need
  • High waist

Cons:

  • Waist may be too high for some
  • Chamios may be too minimal for some

See more at Rapha

Pactimo Range Flyte Cargo

  • 14mm pad
  • 188g (size large)
  • Overlock seams
  • 25cm inseam
  • 24cm center to top
  • 27cm center to top rear
  • Fits true to size, but slightly tight around the thighs
  • Black, Midnight Navy (tested)
  • $199 (on sale for $129 at time of publishing)

The word “racy” comes to mind as I try to summarize the Range Flyte. They’re just as light and sheer as the Rapha Core Cargo, but the fit is a little different. They’re tighter around the thighs and looser around the waist. Both regions were still taught against my skin, but they were more firm against my legs and more comfortable around my belly.

It’s the best application of a design concept shared by all the shorts but the Pearl Izumi Expedition, where the front section of the waist doesn’t have the firmer, thicker extra elastic band that runs along the top of the back and sides. Oddly enough, though, I’d put the Pearl Izumi Expedition in a tie for first in the waist-comfort department. But they were looser-fitting all over. It took a ride and a wash cycle for the Pactimos to kind of “equalize,” but they ended up feeling tight without being uncomfortable

Sparse silicone dots provide traction around the thigh cuffs instead of a nearly wall-to-wall coating like the other three shorts in the mix. The Pactimos should be more friendly to anyone sensitive to chafing or hair-pulling from excessive rubberization. I’d occasionally notice the overlock-style seams (which the Rapha Core Cargo also had) if one bunched up in front of my thigh, but it just took a tug to flatten out and I never noticed it again.

The pockets have the fewest “security measures” in the bunch, but I haven’t had an issue. It’s just that the rounded lower seam and non-reinforced upper edge prevent my phone from feeling truly locked in and bottomed out. And thanks to the aforementioned tightness, loads were the most noticeable on these shorts. But if the load was flat and thin, I still forgot about it in two minutes. And that tightness ensured it wasn’t going anywhere, so it’s

In the saddle, the chamois feels understated much like that of the Rapha Core Cargo, but doesn’t disappear out of the saddle in quite the same way. I think that’s because of its more 3D contoured structure. It does a good job at offering ample padding without overdoing it, though it’s also not as plush as the Pearl Izumi or as well ventilated as the Rapha or MBO. Despite the fact these don’t really stand out on any one specific metric (or perhaps because of it), the Pactimos will probably be my go-to daily drivers, with the Raphas a close second.

Pros:

  • Tight where they need to be, looser where they don’t
  • Techy chamois concentrates plushness where it’s needed
  • Subtle grip at leg cuffs is less grabby

Cons:

  • Chamois has a narrow “sweet spot”

See more at Pactimo

MBO Prime Cargo

  • 14mm chamois thickness
  • 204g (size large)
  • Flatlock seams
  • 23cm inseam
  • 24cm center-to-top
  • 26cm center-to-top rear
  • Fits small
  • Black only
  • $120

These are kind of the wild card of the bunch. MBO (which seriously stands for “Moving Being Open”) ships directly from China. That was almost a deal-breaker, but the non-bib shorts category isn’t bountiful enough for me to be picky. And soon, I reckon Chinese direct-to-consumer manufacturers are going to become more commonplace. But most importantly, these turned out to offer pretty impressive quality. That was clear before I even felt the fabric. They’re packaged in sleek, frosted slide-lock bags and have elegant hang tags tied with black nylon yarn. Their vibe is premium.

But I do have to start with some caveats. Although MBO’s size guide directed me to a US Large / Asia XL, these fit a little tight. A little less than a half size tighter than the Rapha and Pactimo, and not quite a full size tighter than the Pearl Izumi. And on that note, MBO is between production runs, so they don’t expect US XL or US XXLs to be restocked until March of 2027. But there’s no re-design in the works, so this review should stay relevant for a while. And despite my sizing issue, it’s relevant now because there’s plenty more to talk about.

The cut seems to favor a flatter butt. Even with my test shorts’ slightly tighter chassis, I sensed that tightness concentrated across the cheeks. It wasn’t excessive, but I’d say these shorts are not for the caked-up. And the waistband has stouter reinforcement than any other in the test, and that came with more concentrated tension. It’s a bit more traditional in this post-yoga-pant world. Thankfully, the dubious over-stretch method I used on the Raphas helped ease any tight spots I felt. Plus, that reinforcement band is interrupted at the belly, so it limits the tension in the area where it’s most unwelcomed.

There are a few other nice design touches on display here. The pockets have a secure run of elastic edge-banding across the top for peace-of-mind, and the seemingly simple chamois is a nice balance of thin and flat but firm and supportive. But the most notable touch are the perforations at the front of the chamois. I didn’t even notice them until I stood up on a fast descent and I felt a breeze somewhere breezes rarely reach. The rest of the fabric’s breathability seems to be on par with the Pactimo and Rapha, so I can only credit these three little holes. It only makes a difference at speed, but it does make a difference. Maybe that’s where “Moving Being Open” comes from.

Pros:

  • Clever ventilation for the nether-region
  • Most affordable in the bunch (at full price)
  • Traditional but technical waist structure
  • Great option for flat-butts

Cons:

  • Has to ship directly from China
  • Only comes in black

See more at MBO

Pearl Izumi Expedition

  • 18mm chamois thickness
  • 236g (size large)
  • Flatlock seams
  • 23cm inseam
  • 23cm center to top
  • 27cm center to top rear
  • Fits slightly large
  • Black, Dark Navy, Balsam Green, Olive Night (tested)
  • $130 (on sale for $97.50 at time of publishing)

I often say I like when a product “makes choices.” When it doesn’t aim for the middle of the road, but instead picks a lane. The Pearl Izumi Expedition shorts are made for comfort. Of course, “comfort” is relative. For many, a minimalist build and thin chamois are the most comfortable combination. But the Expeditions take a more casual approach. They’re maximalist. They have a wide waistband, an extra pocket and a thick, plush chamois.

Again, they aren’t for everyone, but I like (reasonably) generous pads. I tend to use chamois butter on long rides when excessive surface-area contact might otherwise cause chafing. And I don’t do much pad-free riding. While the Expeditions may not be ideal for hot days, I think they’re ideal for long ones. To be fair, I haven’t torture-tested any other shorts on this list, but my previous pair of Expeditions have taken me on thousands of miles of tours, and have never let me down.

The Expeditions have other long-haul features beyond the chamois. They’re the only non-bib shorts I’ve ever seen with a lumbar pocket. It’s integrated into the waistband itself. You put your cargo through the opening and slide it into the left or right compartment. It’s not very secure, so although it fits a set of keys or a rubber-banded wallet perfectly, I’d never trust either in there. But it’s a great spot for a Clif bar, lightweight gloves, or even a lightweight gilet. It’s nice to have a pocket somewhere less mobile than the thigh, though one of the thigh pockets has another trick up its sleeve.

The right pocket has a secondary mesh sub-pocket that can serve a few purposes. It protects my phone screen if I’m temporarily carrying my keys or a multi-tool in the same pocket. And maybe this is in my head, but it’s a small extra layer of security if I want to carry my wallet in my pocket. Putting it behind that sub-pocket helps prevent it from being dragged out along with whatever’s in the main pocket.

Most importantly, they have an overall “casual” feel. They’re the least race-y in the bunch. I had a hard time making sure the leg cuffs were fully skin-tight, even for the heading photo in this article. But it didn’t bother me on the ride. And the wide waistband had the least noticeable tight spot, despite not having a separate panel at the front without a reinforced rim like all the other non-bib shorts in the bunch. They’re just kinda chill. I put these on and I want to go on a long, easy pedal for a few days.

Pros:

  • Ultra-plush chamois
  • Relaxed fit, especially at the waist
  • Clever second hip pocket
  • Clever back pocket
  • Lots of colors

Cons:

  • Chamois may be too plush for some
  • Fit may be too relaxed for some

See more at Pearl Izumi
